extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate discrete mathematics students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Course project and problem set for an introductory discrete mathematics / computer science class covering binary arithmetic, relay/switch circuit logic, Chinese abacus base exploration, and Pascal's Triangle with proofs using modern notation and mathematical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert 95 to base 2 using Shannon's formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the base 10 number 95 can be written in base 2 using the above formula. In particular, compute ak, sum_{j=0}^k a_j 2^j in terms of addition symbols a_k, a_{k-1}, ..., a_2, a_1, a_0 for the number 95. What is k in this case? Write using the above value for k and each value of a_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show explicit value of k (highest power of 2 needed), list each digit a_j (0 or 1), and write the sum decomposition 95 = sum_{j=0}^k a_j 2^j. Provide the binary string and justify each bit by showing subtraction/division by powers of two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth table for series (plus) operation / interpret as logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider X_ab as a Boolean variable with only two possible values 0 or 1. If X_ab = 0 then the switch is closed and current flows; if X_ab = 1 then the switch is open. Now let X and Y be two Boolean variables. In a table listing all possible values for X and Y, record the results for X + Y when X and Y are joined in series. Be sure to justify your answer by discussing whether current flows in the series circuit. Note whether X + Y corresponds to usual addition and to what extent X + Y represents a construction in logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a full truth table for the series connection (both switches must be closed for current). Explain mapping between electrical behavior (current/no current) and Boolean values and comment on similarities/differences to arithmetic addition and logical conjunction/disjunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth table for parallel (product) operation / interpret as logic
rubrics_metrics.description: In a table listing all possible values for X and Y, record the results for X·Y when X and Y are joined in parallel. Justify your answer by discussing whether current flows in the parallel circuit. To what extent does X·Y represent usual multiplication? To what extent does X·Y represent a construction in logic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full truth table for parallel connection (current flows if at least one branch closed). Explain relationship to arithmetic multiplication and to logical operations (e.g., relate 0/1 mapping to logical OR/AND depending on hindrance convention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate composed circuit and interpret logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a composed circuit using switches X, Y, Z, W (as in the pictured combination), in a table listing all possible values for X, Y, Z and W compute the value (0 or 1) of the circuit. Explain your result in terms of a simple logical construction involving the results for the basic circuits X·Y and X+Y, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the circuit composition by decomposing into basic series/parallel components, produce a full 4-variable truth table, and state the Boolean expression equivalent. Justify each output entry by describing current flow in the diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation truth tables and circuits involving X and X'
rubrics_metrics.description: Define negation X' equal to 1 when X = 0 and 0 when X = 1. In a table listing both values for X compute the value of the circuit consisting of X and X' (single switch pictures provided). In another table compute a different circuit involving X and X'. Can you interpret these tables in terms of simple logical constructions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide truth table for X and its negation and for the given composed circuit(s). Explain how negation behaves electrically and how combinations with a variable and its negation correspond to logical tautologies/contradictions or particular Boolean functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit for ones-place (least significant) digit of binary sum (XOR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a and b be binary variables with one digit. Recall that the digit in the ones place of the arithmetic sum a + b can be expressed using the 'exclusive or' operation. Find a circuit which gives this digit. Justify your answer with a table that lists all possible values of a and b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the gate/circuit equivalent to XOR (or using relays/switches), provide the 2-bit truth table showing the ones-place output, and explain why this corresponds to XOR rather than AND/OR. Note that arithmetic sum and Boolean combination are distinct—explain the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit for twos-place (carry) digit of binary sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a and b be binary variables with one digit. Find a circuit which gives the digit in the twos place (the carry) of the arithmetic sum a + b. Justify your answer using a table listing all possible values of a and b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide circuit implementing the carry (i.e., the AND of a and b for single-bit addition), show the truth table, and explain how this yield matches arithmetic carry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit for middle (twos place) digit of two-bit addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a and b be binary variables with two possible digits. Using Shannon's notation and letting c0 be the carry from the ones-place, determine when the digit in the twos place for the arithmetic sum a + b equals zero vs one. Using a1, b1 and c0 as switches, find a circuit which gives the digit in the twos place for a + b. Justify using a table of all possible values for a1, b1 and c0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the Boolean expression for the middle-bit (e.g., sum bit = a1 XOR b1 XOR c0), design the corresponding circuit, and include a 3-variable truth table demonstrating correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit for fours-place (most significant) digit of two-bit addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a and b be binary variables with two digits. Using a1, b1 and c0 as switches, find a circuit which gives the digit in the fours place (the left-most digit) of a + b. Justify your answer using a table listing all possible values for a1, b1 and c0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the final carry-out expression (e.g., carry-out = majority function or particular combination), provide equivalent relay/switch circuit, and supply a full truth table showing when the most significant bit is 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Chinese abacus carrying operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the library or the world wide web and research how (base 10) addition is performed on an abacus. Pay particular attention to the operation known today as 'carrying.' Notice that representing a number in base 10 requires a minimum of ten distinct values for bead arrangements along a given bar, which includes the value zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how bead manipulations implement unit increments and carries, include step-by-step examples of adding multi-digit numbers on a suan pan, and explain how carries are propagated physically on the device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count distinct bead values per abacus bar and deduce base N
rubrics_metrics.description: On a Chinese abacus, how many distinct numerical values can be represented along a given bar, including the value zero? Let N denote this number of distinct values. If the full range of values for bead arrangements is employed on each bar, what number base is represented on a Chinese abacus?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both upper (five-unit) and lower (one-unit) beads and possible combinations (including using two five-beads). Compute N and state that using N digits per place corresponds to base N positional notation. Show reasoning and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert numbers to base N and tabulate with binary
rubrics_metrics.description: Using N as above, write the base 10 numbers from 1 to 20 inclusive in base N. Invent symbols for additional digits as needed (call them n1, n2, ...), explain symbols, and, in a table, list base 10 numbers 1 through 32 inclusive with their binary equivalents and their base N equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide consistent digit symbol choices, show the conversion algorithm and produce a two-column (or three-column) table: base10, base2, baseN. Explain each conversion step briefly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze pattern between base 2 and base N representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a pattern between the base 2 and base N representations? Explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for relationships when N is a power of 2 (e.g., base16 relates to groups of 4 binary digits) or otherwise; explain structural correspondences (grouping of binary digits) or lack thereof, and justify with examples from the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform addition in base N on abacus and convert
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the number 9 n2 5 n4 in base N (positions given). Explain how to perform the addition 9 n2 5 n4 + n1 7 2 n2 in base N on a Chinese abacus. What is the value of this sum in base N? Convert the final sum to base 10 and explain the conversion process. Extra credit: What is the sum in base 2? Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate addition column-by-column with carries in base N, show intermediate bead manipulations (or equivalent arithmetic), produce final base N result, and then convert to base10 using place-value expansion; for extra credit, convert that base-10 answer to binary or directly perform base-N to binary conversion if N is a power of two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor suitability and enrichment note
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes for the instructor: The project builds naturally on the previous offering 'Binary Arithmetic: From Leibniz to von Neumann,' and is well suited for a first course in discrete mathematics or computer science. The project includes an examination of arithmetic on a Chinese abacus and explores base 16 (hexadecimal) operations on the abacus as an enrichment exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a follow-up or enrichment module; emphasize connections to history (Leibniz, Shannon, von Neumann) and to computer-science practice (hexadecimal shorthand for binary). Encourage hands-on abacus work and comparisons between bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Pascal's rule in Ti,j index notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the notation T_{i,j} to denote the number assigned to the cell in parallel row i and perpendicular row j, explain exactly what Pascal's rule is for determining all the numbers in all the cells. Include full details and explain for exactly which values of the indices he defines the numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the recurrence T_{i,j} = T_{i-1,j} + T_{i,j-1} with appropriate index ranges and base/generator conditions. Specify boundary conditions (first row/column values) and domain of (i,j).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Pascal's terminology in modern notation
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of the notation T_{i,j}, explain Pascal's terms exponent, base, reciprocal, parallel row, perpendicular row, and generator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map Pascal's language to index language (e.g., base n corresponds to set of cells with i+j = n+1 or similar convention used in text), define 'reciprocal' as pair T_{i,j} and T_{j,i}, and explain generator as T_{1,1} or boundary generator value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite Consequences 1 and 2 in Ti,j notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite Pascal's first two 'Consequences' entirely in the T_{i,j} notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence 1: all cells in first parallel row and first perpendicular row equal generator; express as T_{1,j} = G and T_{i,1} = G. Consequence 2: each cell equals sum of cells of preceding parallel row from its perpendicular row to the first, express using summation notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate Pascal's proofs into modern notation verbatim
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite his proofs of these (first two Consequences) word for word in our notation also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a literal translation of Pascal's argument into symbolic/indexed notation preserving the logical flow, including justification of base cases and how recurrence produces the row/column equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically assess Pascal's proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find his proofs entirely satisfactory? Explain why or why not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a critical commentary discussing rigor, generality, clarity, and where modern notation/induction would strengthen or generalize Pascal's arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce improved generalized proofs using modern notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve on Pascal's proofs using our notation. In other words, make them apply for arbitrary prescribed situations, not just the particular examples he lays out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate general statements with explicit quantifiers and ranges, prove using induction or summation notation, and clearly state assumptions (e.g., generator value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove reciprocity/symmetry (Fifth Consequence) in full generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the Fifth Consequence using index notation. Use index notation and Pascal's ideas to prove the Consequence in full generality, not just for the example he gives. Explain the conceptual ideas behind the general proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express reciprocal equality as T_{i,j} = T_{j,i} and provide a proof by induction on i+j or by demonstrating symmetry of the recurrence with symmetric boundary conditions (generator on both margins). Explain conceptual basis (commutativity of addition in recurrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove First Consequence by mathematical induction (teach induction rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Pascal's First Consequence by mathematical induction. (Hint: for a proof by mathematical induction, always first state very clearly exactly what the n-th mathematical statement P(n) says. Then state and prove the base step. Then state the inductive step very clearly before you prove it.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State P(n) precisely (e.g., all entries in row/column n equal generator), show base n=1, then carry out inductive step using recurrence relation. Emphasize structure of induction proof and correct formulation of P(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express and prove Second Consequence with summation notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the general form of Pascal's Second Consequence, and give a general proof using summation notation, following his approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express the statement as T_{i,j} = sum_{k=1}^i T_{k,j-1} (or equivalent depending on indexing), give clear summation-based proof by unfolding recurrence and using boundary values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove Second Consequence by mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Now prove the Second Consequence by mathematical induction, i.e., provide an alternative inductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate induction parameter (e.g., i or base index), state base case, and show inductive step employing recurrence and previously proved facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express Fourth Consequence using summation notation and/or prove by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional: Write the Fourth Consequence using summation notation (hint: can be written using a sum of sums). Try writing Pascal's proof in full generality using summation notation; if you don't complete it his way explain why it is difficult. Optionally prove the Fourth Consequence by mathematical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fourth Consequence: each cell exceeds by unity the sum of all the cells within its parallel and perpendicular rows, exclusive (adjust generator if not unity). Express formally (T_{i,j} = G + sum_{...} ...) and attempt proof either by algebraic manipulation of sums or induction on i+j.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify nth base entries and prove geometric progression of base sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Use T_{i,j} to explain exactly which are the numbers in the n-th base. Write the Seventh Consequence (sum of cells of each base is double that of the preceding base) and its proof in full generality using Ti,j notation. Then write the Eighth Consequence (sum of cells of each base is 2^{n-1} when generator=1) using modern exponential notation and prove it by mathematical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize base n as set {(i,j): i+j = n+1} (or per text indexing), show sum_{i+j=n+1} T_{i,j} = 2^{n-1} (for generator 1) by induction using the recurrence that each base entry is sum of two entries above/left and counting doubling effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite Twelfth Consequence as factorial/binomial formula and prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite Pascal's Twelfth Consequence (ratio of consecutive numbers in a base) as a generalized modern formula entirely in T_{i,j} terminology. Verify correctness on examples from the table. Then adapt Pascal's proof into modern generalized form and use mathematical induction to prove the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express the contiguous ratio T_{i,j+1}/T_{i,j} = (number_of_cells_from_upper_to_top)/(number_of_cells_from_lower_to_bottom) and derive closed-form T_{i,j} = binomial coefficient formula (product of sequences divided by factorial), verify with small (i,j) examples, and provide an induction proof (e.g., using multiplicative form or combinatorial interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute an arbitrary cell by product/quotient method (binomial coefficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Given the perpendicular and parallel exponents of a cell, find its number without making use of the arithmetical triangle. Example: For perpendicular exponent 5 and parallel exponent 3, take numbers 1..4 and 3..6 multiply and divide as shown to obtain the cell number (example gives 15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and justify the product formula (equivalent to binomial coefficient: T_{i,j} = (i+j-2)!/((i-1)!(j-1)! ) times generator) and demonstrate algorithmic steps: multiply numerator sequence and denominator sequence, divide to obtain the entry. Provide derivation from Twelfth Consequence or combinatorial interpretation.
